name: Papyrus sheet
kb: Cut, layered and pressed papyrus strips
note: Papyrus sheets are made by slicing the pith of papyrus stems into thin strips, laying them side by side, then laying a second layer across the first at right angles. The layers are pressed together while still wet, and the plant's own juices glue them without paste. Once dry they form a smooth writing surface.

name: Parchment sheet
note: Parchment is made from animal skin. The skin is soaked in lime, which loosens the hair and fat, then stretched on a frame and scraped with a curved blade while it dries under tension. The result is a smooth, durable sheet that takes ink well and can be scraped clean and written on again.

name: Rag paper sheet
kb: Rag pulp made into sheets by felting
note: Rag paper was invented in China. Rags of hemp and other plant fibre are beaten in water to a fine pulp, and a fine screen is dipped in the pulp and lifted out, so the water drains and the fibres felt together into a sheet. The sheet is pressed only lightly and dried, not pressed hard, which leaves it soft enough to take ink.

name: Quill pen
note: A quill is a large feather whose hollow shaft is cut to a point and slit at the tip. The slit works by capillary action: it holds a small reservoir of ink and draws it down to the point, and light pressure on the writing surface opens the slit to let ink flow. The point wears and roughens quickly, so it must be re-cut every few hours of writing.

name: Steel pen nib
note: A steel pen nib is a thin pointed piece of steel with a slit down the middle. Ink is held in the slit by capillary attraction and flows to the tip as the two halves flex slightly. Nibs are stamped from sheet, pierced, slit, then hardened and tempered so they spring back and do not wear. A quill must be cut again and again by hand, while stamped nibs can be made cheaply in large numbers if the springiness is right.

name: Fountain pen
kb: Sealed ink reservoir with capillary feed and nib
note: Ink reservoir under the nib, with capillary feed. Early designs leak; improved feeds (Waterman, Parker) in the 1880s fix this. Replaces dip pens and quills. Refillable or cartridge designs follow; mass production drives prices down.

name: Graphite pencil
note: A writing stick made of powdered graphite (a soft, black, greasy form of carbon) mixed with clay, shaped into a rod and fired in a kiln, then encased in wood. The more clay in the mix, the harder the lead and the paler the line. Getting the clay-to-graphite ratio and the kiln temperature right took centuries to perfect. It needs pure graphite and a kiln. Poor mixes crumble or smear.

name: Carbon paper
note: Carbon paper is tissue paper coated with a fine layer of carbon dust held in a wax binder. Placed between sheets, the top sheet's writing pressure transfers carbon to the sheet below. The coating must be thin and even to work well without clogging the paper's pores, and the wax keeps the carbon from smudging before you want it to transfer.

name: Iron gall ink
note: Iron gall ink is made by dissolving green vitriol (iron sulphate) in water with an extract of oak galls, which are rich in tannin. The tannin and iron react to form a dark compound that darkens as it meets the air and soaks into the writing surface, so it is hard to wash off. This is why medieval manuscripts in iron gall ink survive, though the acid in it can slowly eat the paper.

name: Printing ink, oil-based
kb: Linseed oil with carbon black, boiled with resin
note: An oil-based ink for printing with metal type, made by boiling linseed oil and mixing in carbon black. It sticks to metal type and transfers cleanly to paper. The non-obvious blocker is that water-based writing ink beads off metal and will not coat the type. It needs a source of oil, a hot fire to heat it and soot or carbon. The thickness of the ink must be right, or it smears or fails to print.

name: Woodblock printing
note: Chinese invention: carving mirror image freehand requires skill. Hardest part is cutting fine lines that do not splinter.

name: Movable type, cast metal
note: Gutenberg's invention was the punch, matrix and adjustable mould that cast thousands of identical letters to same body height.

name: Punch and matrix for type
note: A punch is a hardened steel rod with a single letter cut in relief at its end, in mirror image. Striking it into a softer metal makes a matrix, a cavity that will mould type, and one master punch can make many matrices of the same letter. Each matrix must be struck straight and to a consistent depth so all the cast letters match, which takes extreme precision in hand work.

name: Adjustable type mould
note: A type mould is a two-part brass tool that clamps a matrix at one end and holds a hollow shaped like the body of one piece of type. Its width can be adjusted so narrow and wide letters all cast to the same body height. Molten type metal is poured in and cools quickly, and the halves open so the new type is ejected without deforming. Every piece must come out the same height so the whole page prints evenly.

name: Type metal alloy
kb: Lead-tin-antimony alloy with low melting point and high hardness
note: Type metal is an alloy of lead with tin and antimony. Lead alone is soft and wears quickly, so tin and antimony harden it, and tin also helps it flow into every detail of the mould. Antimony expands slightly as the alloy solidifies, which stops shrinkage leaving the letter faces poorly formed, so the type is sharp and uniform.

name: Composing stick
note: A composing stick is a small hand-held tray in which a compositor sets individual metal letters (sorts) in order, building one line of text at a time. Each finished line is moved to a larger tray called a galley, where a proof is pulled and checked for errors. Letters can be corrected and rearranged until the text is locked into the chase for printing.

name: Chase and forme
note: A chase is an iron frame that holds type, and a forme is the assembled page of type locked inside it. Quoins are wedges driven in against spacers to lock the type so tightly it cannot shift or lift under the press's pressure. Wooden spacers swell and shrink with damp, so the lock must be checked, or the type can come loose and print unevenly.

name: Screw press for printing
note: A press in which a large screw forces a flat plate (platen) down onto the inked type and paper. A long arm turns the screw, and the arm length trades speed for force. The screw threads must be clean and well made or they strip, and parallel guides stop the platen from binding. It needs an accurate screw, wrought iron and good woodwork. Gutenberg's press was of this kind.

name: Iron hand press
note: The iron hand press replaces the wooden screw press with a frame of cast iron, which is strong when squeezed and does not flex like wood, so a larger sheet can be printed at once. A system of levers called a toggle multiplies the pull of the operator's arm most strongly near the end of the stroke, when the paper meets the type. It needs large cast-iron parts of good quality, and the stiffer frame gives a more even impression.

name: Cylinder press
kb: Paper fed between rotating cylinder and flat type bed, steam-driven
note: A printing press in which a rotating cylinder carries the paper across the flat bed of type, pressing it by rolling instead of with a flat plate. Pressure is applied along a line at a time, so a lighter machine can print a larger sheet, faster and smoothly. Steam power drives it, since it is too heavy for hands. It needs a cylinder-boring mill and parts made to fine tolerance.

name: Rotary press
kb: Type or stereotypes on rotating cylinder, paper fed between cylinders, steam-driven
note: A press with two cylinders: type is cast onto a curved plate that wraps around one of them, and the paper feeds continuously between the cylinders from a roll. Printing and delivery never stop, so thousands of sheets per hour can be printed. It needs steam power, curved stereotype plates cast from the type, and a cylinder press as a base. Newspapers depend on it.

name: Stereotype plate
kb: Papier-mache mould of type forme, cast into metal plate, allows curved mounting
note: Papier-mache matrix captures exact impression; pour must be fast. Curved plates enable rotary presses.

name: Electrotype plate
kb: Electroplated copper shell backed with lead, captures type forme detail
note: An electrotype is a copper copy of a printing plate made by electroplating. A mould of the page is taken in wax and coated with graphite so that it conducts, then hung in a copper salt bath with an electric current, and a thin shell of copper slowly builds up on it. The shell is backed with molten lead so it cannot buckle. Copper deposits slowly, but the shell is hard and keeps fine detail.
_internal: [AUDIT: State interest and suspicion were unset and have been defaulted from the category.]

name: Linotype machine
kb: Keyboard-driven machine that casts entire lines of type as single metal slugs
note: A typesetting machine: the operator taps a keyboard, brass moulds (matrices) for each letter drop into a line, spaces are added to fill the line, and hot metal is poured into the moulds so that the whole line is cast as a single solid bar of type. Then the matrices are returned for reuse. It needs electric power, type metal and parts made to close tolerance. It is much faster than setting type by hand.

name: Lithography
kb: Greasy image drawn on limestone, dampened and rolled with oily ink; ink sticks only to image
note: A printing method that works by chemistry, not relief: a design is drawn with greasy ink or crayon on a flat stone, and the stone is treated with acidified water containing alum. The wet stone repels the greasy printing ink, while the greasy design accepts it and rejects water. The chemistry is not obvious, and the stone must be kept damp while it is printed. It needs a flat polished limestone and alum.

name: Chromolithography
note: Colour printing from several lithographic stones, one for each colour, printed one over another. The registration, the alignment between the stones, must be accurate to a fraction of a millimetre, or the picture blurs. A hand-drawn artwork is needed for each colour. It needs lithography and synthetic dyes for brilliant inks. A great deal of skilled labour goes into one picture.

name: Offset lithography
kb: Lithographic image offset onto rubber blanket, then onto paper, allowing curved or small presses
note: In offset lithography the inked image is not printed straight onto paper. It is first transferred from the printing surface to a rubber-covered cylinder, the blanket, which then presses it onto the paper. The soft blanket spares the hard printing surface from wear and prints well on rough paper. The image reverses on the blanket and reverses again on the paper, so the original is drawn the right way round. Rubber blankets are the costly part.

name: Halftone screen and dot matrix
note: THE invention making photographs printable. Cross-ruled screen photographed with image. Variable dots create tone illusion.

name: Photoengraving (relief)
note: Making a metal relief printing plate from a photograph. The image is turned into dots by a halftone screen, light hardens a coating (a photo-resist) on a metal plate where it falls, and acid then eats the unprotected metal between the dots, leaving them raised to print. The height of the dots must be uniform. It needs silver halide photography and acid. Over-etching destroys the finest dots.

name: Typewriter
kb: Keyboard-driven machine that stamps type bars onto paper through ribbon
note: A writing machine with a key for each letter that drives a metal type bar to strike through an inked ribbon onto paper. The QWERTY layout deliberately separates common letter pairs to slow the typist and keep neighbouring bars from jamming. A shift key reaches capitals. It needs steel parts, springs and levers made to interchangeable tolerance. A typist can produce a clean, uniform page.

name: Shift key mechanism
note: A mechanism that lets one key type two characters, such as a small and a capital letter. Pressing the shift key moves the basket of type bars (or the carriage) so that a different part of each type bar strikes the paper. The basket must move reliably without sticking, and the spring return must be precise, or the next keystroke misses. It needs the typewriter and tolerance machining.

name: Stencil duplicator
note: A machine that copies a typed or drawn page: a stencil (a thin sheet coated with a waxy film, cut through by typing) is stretched on a screen, and ink is pressed through the cut parts onto paper. The screen must hold the fabric taut, and register sprockets keep the paper aligned. It wears out after about a few hundred copies. It needs a typewriter, a coating and hand power.

name: Mimeograph
note: A duplicator in which a rotating drum distributes ink evenly through a stencil onto paper fed past it. It is a refined stencil duplicator, driven by hand or power. The stencil wears quickly, but a run can reach a few thousand copies. It needs the stencil duplicator and power. An uneven ink supply gives faint or smeared copies.

name: Case binding
note: Case binding: the pages are sewn in groups (signatures) and the sewing is laced onto cords, then attached to hard boards that form the cover. Sewing is essential for durability, because gluing alone fails within years. Raised bands protect the sewing from shearing. It needs rag paper, leather, thread, glue and board. Weak sewing causes pages to come loose.

name: Camera obscura with lens
kb: Darkened box or room with lens projecting inverted image onto screen or ground glass
note: Lens must be good or image is dim. Pinhole too dim for anything but bright sunlight.

name: Camera lucida
note: A camera lucida is a small prism held on a stand above a sheet of paper. By reflecting light inside the prism, the artist sees the scene and the paper together, as if the scene were laid over the page, and traces its outline with a pencil. The prism has to be made with accurate angles to give a clear view. It needs glass and the skill to shape it, and it lets people who draw poorly make accurate outlines of buildings, landscapes and specimens.

name: Silver halide photographic sensitivity
note: The chemistry behind photography: light breaks down silver halide (a compound of silver with chlorine, bromine or iodine) into specks of silver metal, which is visible once developed. The unexposed halide must be removed without darkening the image, or the whole picture goes dark. It needs silver, pure chemicals and quantitative analysis, and work in darkness.

name: Daguerreotype plate
kb: Polished copper plate coated with silver, sensitised with iodine vapour, exposed and developed with mercury
note: Polished copper plate, silver-coated, exposed to light, developed in mercury vapour. Mirror-like image. Cannot be copied.

name: Calotype paper negative
note: A paper negative made on paper sensitised with silver salts. The negative allows unlimited prints. The paper texture shows in the final image, which softens fine detail. Toning with gold chloride prevents fading. It needs silver halide sensitivity and rag paper. Prints made without proper fixing fade or darken in a few years.

name: Wet collodion plate
kb: Nitrocellulose emulsion on glass, sensitised with silver nitrate, must be exposed and developed wet
note: Glass substrate better than paper. Emulsion must stay wet or sensitivity drops. Field photographers carried dark tents.

name: Dry gelatin emulsion plate
note: Silver halide in gelatin. Sensitive when dry. Long shelf life. Easy storage and transport. Portable photography practical.

name: Celluloid roll film
note: A strip of transparent celluloid (nitrocellulose plastic) coated with photographic emulsion and wound on a spool, with sprocket holes along the edges so frames can be spaced accurately. A roll holds many frames. It enabled amateur photography, since the photographer need not change plates after each shot. It needs a dry gelatin emulsion and fine tolerance machining. Celluloid is flammable.

name: Panchromatic emulsion
note: A photographic emulsion sensitive to all colours of light, including red. The older orthochromatic emulsion sees only blue and green, so red objects come out black. Panchromatic emulsion is sensitised with dyes. It must be handled under dark red or green safelight, not the yellow light that was safe before. It needs dry gelatin plates and synthetic dyes.

name: Autochrome colour plate
note: An early colour photograph process: a glass plate is covered with microscopic grains of starch dyed red, green and blue, and coated with emulsion, so that each grain acts as a tiny colour filter. The result is a transparency that must be viewed with light shining through it. The colours are pastel, and it needs long exposures. It was the only colour process before Kodachrome. It needs a dry gelatin emulsion plate.

name: Flash powder
note: A mixture of magnesium powder and an oxidiser (a chemical that supplies oxygen) that burns in a very brief intense flash for photographing in dark rooms. Magnesium gives a blue-white light closer to daylight than gas lamps. It burns in a fraction of a second. It needs magnesium and corned gunpowder-type chemistry. The flash makes smoke and can burn the photographer, and it is dangerous to keep.

name: Flashbulb
note: A sealed glass bulb filled with oxygen and containing fine metal foil or wire, ignited by electric current to give one bright flash. Because the flash is sealed in, it is safer and cleaner than flash powder. The oxygen must be pure and the bulb sealed; any leak ruins it. Each bulb is used once. It lets shutter speeds rise to a small fraction of a second. It needs a soda-lime glass and electricity.

name: Leaf shutter
note: A camera shutter made of thin overlapping metal blades (leaves) in the lens that open fully and close evenly, timed through gears. It exposes the whole picture at once, so a flash can fire while the blades are open. It needs tolerance machining and accurate screws. If the blades do not open evenly the picture is unevenly exposed.

name: Focal plane shutter
note: A camera shutter that sits right in front of the film: a curtain with a slit travels across the film, and the width of the slit sets the exposure time. For fast speeds the slit must be very narrow, and for the fastest speeds multiple slits are required. It needs tolerance machining, light blind material and springs. Fast-moving subjects can be distorted because the slit exposes one part of the picture after another.

name: Cine camera
note: A movie camera: it takes a series of still photographs on roll film, each frame held still for a moment while the shutter is open and then pulled forward by a sprocket. The intermittent movement must be reliable. The drive is by spring or motor, and a motor gives steadier speed. It needs celluloid roll film and tolerance machining. Uneven speed makes the movement look jerky when projected.

name: Intermittent film movement
kb: Rotating Maltese cross cam drives film advance pin intermittently, pausing for exposure
note: Cross slots must be precise or pin binds. Smooth during pull-down allows high speed.

name: Film projector
note: A machine that shows movie film: a lamp and lens throw each frame onto a screen. A shutter blanks the light while the film is pulled down to the next frame, so the viewer does not see blur and no flicker appears. A gate holds the film flat. It needs celluloid roll film and ground lenses. Heat from the lamp can set the film on fire, so heat dissipation is critical.

name: Phonautograph
note: A device that records sound as a wavy line: a horn collects sound, which moves a diaphragm and a stylus that traces the vibrations onto a soot-blackened cylinder or paper. It records sound but cannot play it back. The stylus must be flexible but not break. It needs fine metalwork. It proved that sound can be written, and it led to recording that can be replayed.

name: Tin foil phonograph
note: The first machine that could both record and play back sound. A stylus attached to a diaphragm indents a groove in a sheet of tin foil wrapped around a rotating cylinder; to replay, the stylus rides in the groove and moves the diaphragm. Playback is faint. The foil crinkles after a few plays and is quickly worn. It needs aluminium or tin foil and the phonautograph's design.

name: Wax cylinder record
note: A recording cylinder made of wax, which a stylus cuts more cleanly than it indents foil. It sounds better and survives many plays. The surface can be shaved off and recoated, so a cylinder can be used again. Playback is by a needle riding in the groove and vibrating a diaphragm. It needs beeswax and a better stylus. Copies cannot be made easily; each is an original recording.

name: Disc record
note: A flat record with a spiral groove that wobbles from side to side, the wobble encoding the sound's loudness. Shellac discs are pressed from a master, so many copies can be made from one recording, which cylinders could not do. It needs shellac, a wax cylinder recording system and a press. The master must be made carefully, because every copy repeats its flaws.

name: Acoustic horn recording
note: Recording by gathering sound with a large horn that drives a diaphragm and cutting stylus directly, with no electricity. Horn gain is logarithmic, the frequency response is lumpy and bass is absent. The diaphragm's compliance (its give) limits the force it can apply to the stylus. It needs the disc record and fine metalwork. Performers must crowd round the horn.

name: Gramophone motor and governor
note: A spring motor with a governor that turns the record at a steady speed. Speed variation ruins the pitch, so a centrifugal governor (weights that fly outward as it speeds up) adjusts a brake or throttle to hold it constant, and a flywheel smooths the ripple. It needs a disc record and machine work. A worn spring or governor makes music wander in pitch.

name: Carbon microphone
note: A microphone that uses a small chamber of carbon granules between two plates. Sound moves a diaphragm, which squeezes the granules and changes the electrical resistance, so the current through them varies with the sound. The packing pressure is critical: if too loose, sensitivity falls. The lifetime is short, because the granules settle and pack. It needs a battery, carbon black and a diaphragm.

name: Moving coil loudspeaker
note: A loudspeaker in which a coil of wire attached to a paper cone sits in a magnetic field; the signal current makes the coil move, pushing the cone and the air. The paper cone has resonances, which colour the sound, and large speakers smooth out the response. Its impedance (resistance to alternating current) is low, so the amplifier must match it. It needs an electromagnet and rag paper.

name: Magnetic tape recording
note: Recording on steel wire or tape coated with magnetic powder: a recording head magnetises it in a pattern matching the sound, and a playback head reads that pattern back. It can be erased and reused, and the response is more even than a disc. It needs electromagnets, paper or plastic for the tape, and electrical amplification. It makes editing possible.

name: AC bias for tape recording
note: A high-frequency signal added to the audio signal in tape recording so the tape is magnetised in a linear way. Without bias, distortion is severe. The bias frequency lies above the range of hearing, and the bias level is critical: too little gives distortion and too much loses high notes. It needs a magnetic tape recorder and an oscillator.

name: Disc cutting lathe
note: A lathe for cutting the master disc. A cutting stylus driven by the recorded signal moves across a rotating disc and the spiral feed pitch must be precise. The speed must be constant or the pitch wavers, and wear on the stylus is compensated for. It needs electric power and a screw-cutting lathe with a lead screw. Flaws in the master are copied into every disc.

name: Electric telegraph
kb: Key switch closes electromagnet circuit, solenoid pulls armature clicking against stop
note: Single needle precedes this. Relay allows weak signal to switch strong at repeater.

name: Morse key and sounder
note: The sender's key closes the telegraph circuit in short and long pulses (dots and dashes) which spell letters in Morse code; the receiver's sounder is an electromagnet that clicks as the current is switched, and operators learn to read the clicks by ear. Sounder design affects how easily operators learn; an American style is fast and bright. It needs an electric telegraph, a battery and a trained operator.

name: Telegraph relay
note: A switch worked by an electromagnet on a long telegraph line: the weak current arriving from the far end moves an armature which switches a local battery, regenerating a strong signal to send on. Chained relays allow unlimited range. It needs an electromagnet and battery. Contacts burn if they are dirty, so they must be kept clean and adjusted.

name: Submarine cable with gutta percha
_internal: [GATE: Rides on the running telegraph network (lines, operators, cells); with the network shut it has nothing to carry.]
note: The insulation IS the invention. Rubber perishes and cotton is useless wet, but gutta percha, the latex of Palaquium from Malaya, is thermoplastic: it softens in hot water, can be moulded round a copper core, sets hard, and does not rot in seawater. It is reached by extending east whatever long-distance ocean trade route you already have (Rome already sails to India annually; adapt to your own reach), so it is a trading problem, not an impossibility. The second, harder lesson is electrical: a long submerged cable is a capacitor, pulses smear into each other, and pushing more voltage at it destroys the insulation, which is what killed the first Atlantic cable in 1858. Signal slowly and detect sensitively.

name: Cable repeater and amplifier
note: A device on a long cable that receives a weak signal and boosts it so it can carry on. It extends the range of a submarine cable from a short run to a much longer one. It needs a telegraph relay and a submarine cable insulated with gutta percha. Submerged repeaters are very hard to maintain, because a fault means raising the cable from the sea bed.

name: Telephone transmitter
note: The part of a telephone that turns the speaker's voice into an electrical signal: a carbon microphone placed close to the mouth. It is louder than a simple mouthpiece, but is prone to feedback with a loud receiver. It needs a constant voltage supply, as a carbon microphone only works with current flowing. It needs a carbon microphone as a base.

name: Telephone receiver
note: The part of a telephone that turns the electrical signal back into sound: an electromagnet pulls a thin iron diaphragm in step with the current, making it vibrate and sound. The fidelity is poor; only a narrow band of speech frequencies pass. Its impedance must match the line and handset. The movement of the diaphragm is small. It needs an electromagnet and a thin iron plate.

name: Telephone exchange and switchboard
note: A switchboard where operators connect telephone lines so any subscriber can reach any other. Without one every pair of telephones would need its own wire. An operator listens to the caller, plugs a cord into the right socket and rings the other. The operator can hear both parties and must avoid feedback. Capacity is limited by the number of operators. It needs a telegraph relay and a telephone transmitter.

name: Strowger automatic exchange
note: A caller dials pulses on the handset (1=one pulse, 2=two pulses, etc). These pulses drive a stepper motor which rotates a wiper across a grid of contacts, selecting the called party's line. No human operator needed. The 1890 Strowger exchange was a mechanical marvel: 100 stepper units could handle 10,000 lines. Reliability was marginal (mechanical wear, misalignment), but no wage bill. Replaced manual exchanges over 30 years. The real innovation is replacing human labor with electromechanics.

name: Loading coil
kb: Inductance coil added to telephone line at intervals, reduces attenuation, extends range
note: Extends range from 20 to 50 km. Wrong spacing causes new problems. Crosstalk increases.

name: Spark transmitter
note: An early radio transmitter: an electric spark jumps a gap and sets a tuned circuit (a coil and capacitor) ringing, and the circuit radiates radio waves. The emission is a damped wave, dying away after each spark, which is spread over a wide band. The spark gap erodes, and a motor-driven rotating gap keeps the wear even and prevents pitting. It needs a tuned circuit, a high voltage supply and an antenna.

name: Coherer detector
note: A tube of glass filled with iron filings between two metal plugs. When RF current (from a radio signal) passes through, the filings cohere (stick together), dropping resistance from 1 megohm to 1000 ohms. A relay responds to this current change, signalling the received dot or dash. After each signal, a tapper mechanically shakes the tube to decohere the filings. Unreliable and slow (tapping delay), but it was the only radio detector before solid-state rectifiers.

name: Crystal detector
note: A detector that picks the audio signal out of radio waves using a crystal, such as galena (lead sulfide), touched by a fine wire called a cat's whisker. The contact point conducts better in one direction, so it rectifies (cuts off half the wave). The whisker must be pressed precisely. It is temperamental to adjust, but much more reliable than the coherer, an earlier detector.

name: Tuned LC circuit
kb: Inductor and capacitor in series or parallel; resonance at specific frequency
note: Resonance sharpest with low resistance; high Q demands low loss. Variable capacitor tunes band.

name: Continuous wave transmitter
note: A radio transmitter producing a steady, unbroken wave, not the bursts of a spark transmitter. A continuous wave takes a narrower band of frequencies, so more stations fit together. It needs regenerative circuits (which feed output back to sustain oscillation) and tubes. Frequency drift is a problem, since the frequency changes with temperature and tuning. It is the basis of voice broadcasting.

name: Triode oscillator
note: A triode with feedback can generate any frequency from audio (10 Hz) to microwave (1000 MHz), tuned by the LC circuit. The oscillation amplitude is limited by the triode's power supply and efficiency. Used in radio transmitters, local oscillators for superheterodyne receivers, and audio oscillators for music synthesis. The triode is THE electronic oscillator until solid-state transistors arrive.
_internal: [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_vac_1e3 added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: vacuum tube oscillator needs high vacuum for electron operation]

name: Amplitude modulation
note: A microphone signal (audio, 0-10 kHz) is added to the RF oscillator output, varying its amplitude. The modulated wave is transmitted; a receiver detects the envelope (the modulation) using a rectifier, recovering audio. The trick: a 1 MHz carrier modulated with 1 kHz audio produces sidebands at 999 kHz and 1001 kHz. Radio stations are spaced 10 kHz apart (AM broadcast). The bandwidth is about 2x the audio frequency. Simple and robust.

name: Superheterodyne receiver
note: Instead of amplifying the RF signal directly (hard at high frequencies), a mixer combines the received signal with a local oscillator, producing a difference frequency (intermediate frequency, typically 455 kHz or 10.7 MHz). Tuning changes only the local oscillator; the intermediate frequency is fixed and easy to amplify. This is the most important radio innovation after AM: it made high-gain, selective receivers practical. Nearly all radio since 1920 is superheterodyne.

name: Frequency modulation
note: Audio signal varies the frequency of the RF carrier instead of the amplitude. A 100 MHz carrier modulated with 1 kHz audio swings ±75 kHz. FM is immune to amplitude noise (static, ignition noise), so reception is much quieter. Bandwidth is about 10x wider than AM (200 kHz for 15 kHz audio), requiring wider channel spacing. Requires sophisticated receivers (discriminators, limiters). Adopted late (1940s in consumer radio) due to infrastructure cost, but ultimately superior.

name: Dipole antenna
note: A radio antenna made of two equal rods or wires in a line, fed in the middle. It radiates and receives at the frequency for which its length is about half a wavelength. Its radiation resistance is low, so matching to the transmitter is essential. A high overhead antenna matters most; the ground connection is less important. It needs a tuned circuit and wire. A wrong length reduces range sharply.

name: Radio direction finding
note: Finding the direction of a radio transmitter by turning a loop or directional aerial until the signal fades to a null. A null is sharper than a maximum, so it is the better indicator. The bearing error is a few degrees. Two direction finders at different places draw lines that cross at the transmitter, so a position is triangulated. It needs a superheterodyne receiver.

name: Radar
kb: Pulse transmitter and receiver with CRT display, shows range and bearing to reflective objects
note: Pulse timing must be precise. CRT displays return. Critical for aircraft detection. Extremely difficult.

name: Cathode ray tube
note: An evacuated glass tube with a heated cathode that emits electrons, accelerated by 10,000 V towards a phosphor-coated anode. The electron beam is steered by magnetic coils (X and Y deflection). Where the beam hits the screen, the phosphor glows. Varying the beam current modulates the brightness. This is the display technology that made electronic television possible. The key: the beam is fast (MHz), allowing full-screen raster scanning at video rate.
_internal: [REVIEWED: prerequisite(s) cap_vac_1e3 added by a reviewer working node by node. Reason: evacuated tube for electron beam display requires high vacuum]

name: Television by mechanical scanning
note: Television that scans a picture with a spinning perforated disc (a Nipkow disc), which breaks the image into lines. A light sensor such as a selenium cell measures each point, and a matching disc at the receiver rebuilds the picture. The disc must rotate precisely in step, flicker is a problem at low frame rates, and the picture is extremely dim. It needs a camera obscura lens and a selenium photovoltaic cell.

name: Iconoscope camera tube
note: An electronic television camera tube: a lens focuses the scene on a mosaic of tiny light-sensitive cells in a vacuum tube, which store charge, and an electron beam scans them one by one. The mosaic must have a fine structure, and the capacitive coupling to each cell is critical. It needs a cathode ray tube and a camera lens. It replaced mechanical scanning because it has no moving parts and is much brighter.

name: Video scanning standard
note: An agreed set of rules for how a television picture is scanned: the number of lines, the frame rate and the synchronisation pulses that let the receiver lock on to the sender. The frame rate is matched to the power line frequency to avoid hum bars. It needs an iconoscope camera and a cathode ray tube. Adoption is slow, because every sender and every receiver must follow the same standard.

name: Facsimile transmission
note: Sending a picture or document over a wire or by radio by scanning it line by line, converting the brightness to an electrical signal and rebuilding it at the receiver. The sender and receiver must be in perfect synchronisation. Scanning speed trades resolution for time: a fine picture takes longer. It needs a selenium photovoltaic cell and amplitude modulation. Out of step, the picture is sheared.

name: Punched card
note: A stiff card with holes punched in set positions to record data, read by mechanical sensing: pins or brushes pass through the holes. The format of 80 columns by 12 rows became a de facto standard. It needs rag paper (stout card stock) and tools to punch holes precisely. Information is stored as holes that machines can sort, count and compare. Damp cards swell and jam.

name: Jacquard card chain
note: A chain of punched cards fed through a loom, with each card controlling which warp threads are lifted for one row of the pattern. It reduces the work of weaving complex patterns, and thousands of cards weave complicated fabrics such as brocade. It needs the punched card. It is a precursor of computing, because it is a stored programme controlling a machine.

name: Hollerith tabulator
note: A machine that reads punched cards and counts the data on them: reading brushes or pins sense the hole positions, and each hole closes an electric circuit that advances a dial counter. Census processing time fell from years to weeks. It needs punched cards and a card sorter, with electric contacts made carefully. Dirty contacts cause miscounts.

name: Card sorter
note: A machine that sorts punched cards into bins according to the holes in a chosen column. A reading device senses the hole and a solenoid (an electromagnet with a plunger) moves a gate that sends the card to the right bin. The plunger must be fast and strong, and cards must not jam. It sorts at a rate of cards per second. It needs punched cards and electromagnets.

name: Keypunch machine
note: A machine with a keyboard that punches holes in cards: the operator presses a key and a punch makes the matching holes in the card held under it. The card must be held precisely during the punch, and the operator verifies the key before the strike. Jams are common. It needs a typewriter and punched cards, and the work needs a trained operator.

name: Adding machine
note: A mechanical calculator for adding columns of numbers. Digit wheels, one for each decade, turn as keys are pressed, and the carry mechanism passes a carry from each wheel to the next. The carry is critical: each decade must propagate carry. It adds only, and does not multiply. It needs gears cut to fine tolerance and a crank and linkage for power.

name: Comptometer
note: Instead of a crank (one operation per second), the Comptometer (1887 onward) uses keys (one per digit). Pressing a key lever multiple times increments that digit, accumulating the sum. Touch typists could use Comptometers almost as fast as they thought of numbers. Faster than Arithmometer. The innovation is that the operator interface is ergonomic and intuitive (press 5 five times to add 5), not just mechanical optimization.

name: Cash register
note: A machine that records each sale as it is made: an adding mechanism totals the amounts, a bell rings, the drawer opens, and a counter records every transaction on a roll. A mechanical register prevents the clerk from under-ringing (not recording a sale and pocketing the money). A solenoid locks the drawer. It needs the adding machine and electromagnets. It was meant to stop theft by staff.

name: Slide rule
note: Two wooden rules with logarithmic scales, aligned by hand and compared visually. To multiply 5*7, you find 5 on one scale and 7 on the other, align them, and read 35 off the fixed scale. Uses the log identity: log(a*b)=log(a)+log(b). Accuracy is 3 digits, good enough for engineering work. Ubiquitous by 1900, slide rules were the dominant calculation tool until electronic calculators (1970s). Simple, cheap, and fast enough for design iteration.

name: Index card and filing system
note: A filing system of standard-sized cards, each holding a single entry, kept in drawers in order. The cards can be added, removed and reordered at any time, which is an improvement over bound ledgers, in which a new entry cannot be inserted. The standard card size is three by five inches. Discipline in keeping the filing order is essential. It needs rag paper and cabinets made to tolerance.

name: Dewey decimal classification
note: A scheme for classifying library books by subject number, written as decimals. It is hierarchical: the main classes are divided into divisions, and then into sections, and each digit narrows the subject. It allows new books to be inserted without renumbering the others. It needs an index card and filing system. Its categories reflect the knowledge of its time, so new fields fit awkwardly.
